source.publisher: Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI), HM Treasury
source.title: Financial Services Threat Assessment

summary: OFSI's February 2025 sector assessment finds that, since the UK's February 2022 Russia sanctions expanded, Russian designated persons (DPs) have increasingly relied on new professional and non-professional enablers to breach UK financial sanctions. Enabler activity falls into three categories: making payments through UK banks and NBPSPs to maintain DPs' lifestyles and assets (superyachts, UK residential properties); fronting to claim ownership of frozen assets; and other money laundering, including cryptoasset-to-fiat conversion, to give DPs liquidity, with one disrupted network exposed to the designated exchange Garantex and Tether (USDT). The report also flags common compliance failures (frozen-asset maintenance, licence breaches, ownership and UK-nexus assessment errors, and exposure to Russia's SPFS messaging alternative) and identifies a set of intermediary jurisdictions -- including BVI, Cyprus, Switzerland, UAE, Austria, Turkiye and the Cayman Islands -- that recur in suspected breach reports, each associated with specific risk activities such as enabler activity, non-resident banking, opaque corporate/trust structures and crypto transactions.

extraction_notes: Document states (p.5) that all named individuals, entities and case studies are fictional, illustrative constructs; accordingly, the named case-study parties (Company X/Y/Z, Manager Y, Global Bank, Neo-Bank, Seafarer Z, Associate, Company L/L Investments/L Capital, Company Rus, Company A, Company UK, Individual S, Individual M) were NOT extracted as real-world actors -- only the underlying category actors (DPs, professional/non-professional enablers) and the two real, named entities (Garantex, NCA) were captured. SPFS/correspondent-banking exposure (p.11) is a single narrative mention rather than a developed typology and was captured only as an indicator, not proposed as a standalone typology. Jurisdiction list mixes those where DPs/enablers are based (RU, GB) with the eight named 'intermediary jurisdictions' (p.25-27) and the other sanctions regimes referenced in the threat overview (Libya, Belarus, Iran, DPRK, p.8); it does not imply sanctions breaches occurred in each. Reviewer should confirm desk routing, particularly whether markets_desk/crypto-specific routing is warranted for the CMI010 link.
